theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Sacraments, The Lord’s Supper
summary: The meaning, nature, and practice of the Lord’s Supper; participation in Christ; the new covenant meal
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, Luke 22:14-20, and Matthew 26:26-29. Today is a doctrinal pause on the Lord’s Supper. Notice what Jesus said and did, and how Paul corrects the Corinthians’ abuse of the meal.
settingTheScene: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus celebrated the Passover with his disciples and gave them a new meal. From the beginning the church repeated this meal. By the time Paul wrote, it was a regular part of church gatherings. In Corinth, the meal had been corrupted: the rich ate and drank to excess while the poor went hungry, so the meal became a mark of division, not unity. Paul’s correction tells us what the Supper is meant to be.
observation: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).
“This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).
“This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).
“For this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28).
“I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29).
“For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).
“Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28).
“For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).
doctrinalFocus:
The Lord’s Supper (also called Communion, the Eucharist, or the Lord’s Table) is the meal in which Christ’s people eat bread and drink the cup in remembrance of his death. Jesus instituted it at the Last Supper, and the church has observed it since the first century. It has several meanings. It looks back: “Do this in remembrance of me.” It proclaims: “You proclaim the Lord’s death.” It looks forward: “until he comes,” and Jesus pointed to the feast in the kingdom. It signifies and seals the new covenant in his blood, the forgiveness of sins. And it signifies our unity: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

Christians have disagreed about how Christ is present in the Supper, and this is one of the major differences between traditions. Roman Catholics hold that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation). Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with, and under” the elements. Reformed Christians (following Calvin) hold that Christ is truly present by the Spirit, and the believer feeds on him by faith, though not physically in the elements. Many Baptists and others hold that the Supper is primarily a memorial and proclamation, an ordinance in which Christ is remembered. Traditions also differ on who may partake, how often, and who may administer. These matters deserve serious study and respect for one another.

What all agree on is that the Supper is a gift of grace for believers and a means of strengthening faith. It is to be approached with self-examination, not to earn forgiveness but to repent, trust, and be reconciled. It is to be shared in a way that honors the unity of the body. And it points beyond itself: the table is a foretaste of the wedding supper of the Lamb.
interpretation:
In Luke 22, Jesus says, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” He knew what lay ahead and still longed for fellowship with his friends. The Passover meal remembered God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt, with the blood of a lamb protecting the firstborn. Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says, “This is my body, which is given for you.” After supper he takes the cup: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” Matthew adds, “for the forgiveness of sins.” He is the Lamb, and his blood establishes the new covenant that Jeremiah promised (31:31-34). And he looks ahead: he will not drink again until he drinks it new in the kingdom.

In 1 Corinthians 11, Paul first rebukes the divisions at the meal: “When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.” They were humiliating the poor. Then he recalls what he received from the Lord: Jesus on the night he was betrayed took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, “This is my body which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise the cup. The Supper is a proclamation of the Lord’s death.

Paul warns: “Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.” The “unworthy manner” refers to how they ate, with contempt for the poor, not that the person is unworthy, since no one is worthy in himself. “Let a person examine himself, then.” We examine our hearts and our relationships. Some had become weak, ill, or had died, as a disciplinary judgment from the Lord, “that we may not be condemned along with the world.” It is a sober reminder. The right response is not to avoid the table but to come repentant and in unity: “When you come together to eat, wait for one another.”

Taking the Supper is one of the plainest ways the gospel is displayed. We do not make the meal; we receive it. We do not offer a sacrifice; we receive the benefits of the one sacrifice. And we eat together, which shows that we are one family.
connection: Exodus 12 describes the Passover. Exodus 24:8 speaks of the blood of the covenant. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant. John 6:22-59 is Jesus’ bread of life discourse. 1 Corinthians 10:14-22 speaks of participation. Isaiah 25:6-8 pictures the feast on the mountain. Revelation 19:6-9 describes the marriage supper of the Lamb. Acts 2:42 and 20:7 show the early church breaking bread. Hebrews 9:11-10:18 explains the once-for-all sacrifice. Matthew 5:23-24 speaks of reconciliation before worship.
application:
Before your next Communion, spend time examining your heart. Ask whether you are at peace with others.

Read the words of institution slowly and picture the upper room.

Pray for unity in your church and for those in your church who are poor or left out.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for the bread and the cup.
Ask him to teach you to come to his table with reverence and joy.
Ask him to remind you of his death until he comes.
